Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

issues.item: Expressions of Affection: Physical affection such as hugs
issues.explanation: These trigger items are not clinically coherent with the indexed trauma of mugging/robbery. Physical affection such as hugs is difficult to connect to robbery-related threat activation without any supporting appraisal, memory, or strategy content, and it conflicts with the otherwise stranger/sudden-movement threat profile. Crash imagery is more characteristic of road traffic trauma than robbery and lacks any plausible link to the reported threat items.

issues.item: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: The trigger item about cars being hit in an accident is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of mugging/robbery. The other trigger and threat items coherently suggest interpersonal danger and hypervigilance around strangers/crowding, but crash imagery points to a motor vehicle trauma theme that is not reflected elsewhere in the profile or in the cognitive formulation. This is more than unusual; it appears to reference a different trauma context.

vignette:
Ramesh, a 76-year-old South Asian man and retired electrician, still carried the wiry tension of a man who had spent decades reading a live wire's danger. That vigilance had once served him well on job sites across Chicago, but it had warped into something else one autumn evening last year. He had been walking home from the corner store, a bag of onions in one hand, when two young men stepped out from behind a parked van. One of them smelled sharply of alcohol. They shoved him against a brick wall, demanded his wallet, and when he fumbled, one punched him in the ribs. Ramesh remembered the sour smell of the man's breath, the way the brick scraped his cheek, and the terrible, helpless realization that he was old and slow and alone. They took thirty-seven dollars and left him crumpled on the sidewalk. For weeks afterward, he could not walk past that corner without his chest tightening.

The first nightmares came a few nights later. He would jolt awake at 3 a.m., heart hammering, the smell of alcohol thick in his nostrils even though the bedroom was empty. His wife, Priya, would reach for him, but he would lie rigid, staring at the ceiling, waiting for a threat that never came. The dream residue clung to him through the morning, a film of dread that made him irritable and withdrawn. He began to notice that crowded places-the grocery store, the bus stop, even the temple on festival days-felt unbearable. Every stranger's approach seemed charged with potential violence. A man stepping too close at the pharmacy checkout would make Ramesh's hand twitch toward his pocket, searching for a wallet that no longer held anything worth stealing.

The threat felt most acute at night. After sundown, Ramesh would lock every door twice, check the windows, and pull the curtains so tight that no streetlight leaked through. He found himself sitting in the dark living room, listening to the creak of the house, certain that someone was out there. He stopped taking evening walks with Priya, a ritual they had shared for forty years. She did not understand why he now insisted she be home before dark, or why he flinched when their grandson ran up behind him too quickly. A sudden movement from anyone-a child, a neighbor, a man reaching into his own jacket for a phone-would make Ramesh freeze, his body flooding with adrenaline before his mind could catch up.

What frightened Ramesh most was not the memory of the robbery itself, but the sense that the world had become a place where danger could erupt from any ordinary moment. A whiff of alcohol on a bus passenger's breath would send him straight into a cold sweat, his mind replaying the shove, the scrape, the punch. He had come to believe that strangers were not just unpredictable but actively threatening, and that his only safety lay in constant watchfulness. This belief was strongest at night, when the dark felt like a cover for anyone who might be coming for him.

By the time he finally agreed to see a therapist, at Priya's gentle but persistent urging, Ramesh had not left the house after 5 p.m. in three months. He spent his days in the backyard, tinkering with old tools, his back to the fence. He was afraid of what would happen if he let his guard down even for a moment. He was also, quietly, afraid that he was losing the man he used to be-someone who fixed things, who walked home without thinking, who did not see a threat in every stranger's face.
